paras: The lynching of John Johnson was the hanging of a 17-year-old Black youth by a crowd at Rock Hill, South Carolina, early on the morning of June 12, 1882. Johnson had been accused of assaulting Alice McDowell, a white girl, the day before, and was taken from a guard and hanged from a tree on Main Street. A coroner's jury found that he was hanged by persons unknown, and a Charleston wire carried the news to papers across the country.

According to a Rock Hill dispatch dated June 11, McDowell was hunting for plums with other children that Sunday morning when she was "seized and assaulted" by Johnson. Her companions fled and gave the alarm, and Johnson was caught. The same dispatch said he had confessed and added that he "will probably be lynched."

A local account from the Register, reprinted by the Abbeville Press and Banner, said Johnson was confronted with the girl, who identified him, after which he confessed and was lodged in the guard house. It described him as from Chester County and employed for about a month by J. R. Allen, a merchant. Reports gave McDowell's age as 15, 16 or "about 13."

At about 1 A.M. on Monday, June 12, a crowd of "some hundred men" overpowered the guard who held Johnson at the guard house. They took him to Main Street, where he was found hanging from a tree with a placard on his breast reading "Our women shall be protected." Later that day the body was cut down and placed in a shed near the guard house.
An inquest was held at the shed, and the jury returned a verdict that Johnson was hanged by persons unknown. No report of an arrest or prosecution of any member of the crowd appears in the coverage.

The news spread chiefly through a two-line Charleston dispatch stating that "the negro John Johnson, who outraged Miss McDowell" at Rock Hill had been "lynched this morning." Washington's Evening Star ran it on June 12, and over the next days it appeared in Memphis, Sacramento, Salt Lake City, Eureka and Somerset, Pennsylvania, often beside the Mississippi lynching of a man named Beckett. Headlines ranged from the flat "Lynched This Morning" to the National Republican's "Another Scoundrel to Hang" and the Memphis Daily Appeal's "Another Black Fiend Swung Up."

Every report treated the accusation as established fact, and none questioned the lynching. The Farmer and Mechanic of Raleigh remarked that "the Rock Hill men are not given to waste time fooling with court proceedings in such cases." The Abbeville Press and Banner wrote that such offenders forfeited their lives to "the stern demands of justice," and dismissed the account of overpowered guards, masked men and a verdict against parties unknown as "the usual story."

Weekly papers in Kentucky, Ohio, Wisconsin and Dakota later reduced the case to one-line items, some without a name or place, such as the Maysville Evening Bulletin's "A colored scoundrel was lynched in South Carolina, Monday." The Hand County Press counted it among three lynchings in one day as evidence that lynching was "becoming a common occurrence." No Black-press account was found.

Short reprints garbled details: the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian placed the lynching "at Charleston," the wire's dateline, and the Evening Star and St. Paul Daily Globe placed Rock Hill in North Carolina. The Huntsville Gazette and the Bourbon News said Johnson was taken from a jail, while the local Register account says guard house. The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer alone said he was lynched for the "murder" of McDowell, where fuller reports speak of an outrage.

The Charleston wire (A4, A9, A10) and a separate local Register account reprinted in Abbeville (A15) agree that Johnson was hanged by a mob at Rock Hill early on June 12.
